stories.title: As Fed Hikes Rates for First Time Since 2023, Commercial Real Estate Comes to Terms
stories.excerpt: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years Wednesday, but the hawkish move is not expected to curtail commercial real estate transactions in the latter half of 2026. In a unanimous 12-0 vote, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) hiked its benchmark interest rate a quarter point to between 3.75 percent and 4 percent, noting continued inflationary pressures that have been compounded by the war in Iran. The move followed five straight rate holds and marked the central bank’s first time increasing borrowing costs since July 2023. The Fed also released its updated quarterly “dot plot” matrix of individual committee members, which signaled an additional rate hike later this year would likely be supported by 16 of 18 FOMC participants. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has not participated in the dot plot exercise since taking over the leadership post in June. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long,” Warsh said in a post-meeting press conference. “This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.” The FOMC said it remains committed to maintaining the board’s long-standing inflation goal of a 2 percent annual rate, and that recent data put the rate well above this target. The Fed’s dot plot grid projected the federal funds rate at 4.1 percent for the end of 2026 and remain at that level through 2027. Since assuming the Fed chair post from Jerome Powell, Warsh has presided over two pauses and one rate hike in his first three meetings as Fed chair despite external pressure from President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh in January. In a Sept. 4 Truth Social post, Trump called on the Fed to cut interest rates or he would stop trading with certain countries. bullets: Fed raises rates 25 bps to 3.75–4% Wednesday, first hike since July 2023.
16 of 18 FOMC members signal additional rate increase likely later in 2026.
CRE transaction activity expected to continue despite hawkish stance through H2 2026.
stories.summary: The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter point to 3.75–4% Wednesday, citing persistent inflation compounded by geopolitical tensions. The move marks the first rate increase in more than three years and breaks a streak of five consecutive holds. Fed guidance signals 16 of 18 policymakers expect at least one more quarter-point hike by year-end, with some projecting two additional moves in 2026. Despite the hawkish pivot, industry observers expect CRE dealmaking to remain active through the latter half of 2026.
stories.impact: Rate increases compress cap rates and raise borrowing costs, reducing property valuations and development feasibility across all multifamily markets. Rising rates particularly pressure bridge and mezzanine financing, forcing developers to lengthen holds or seek alternative capital structures. Watch for underwriting stress in secondary markets with weaker absorption and rent growth; primary coastal metros with strong job growth may absorb the shock more easily.

stories.title: Law Firm Greenberg Traurig Expands to 133K SF at One Vanderbilt
stories.excerpt: Law firm Greenberg Traurig has no objections to its Midtown offices at One Vanderbilt — in fact, it’s taking even more space there. The law firm, which provides legal services to businesses, financial institutions and high-profile individuals, has signed a 10.5-year lease for 33,477 additional square feet on the entire 33rd floor of SL Green Realty’s trophy high-rise at 1 Vanderbilt Avenue, according to the landlord. The lease brings Greenberg’s total office footprint at the skyscraper to 133,365 square feet. Greenberg signed its initial 15-year lease for four contiguous floors at One Vanderbilt in January 2018, before the 1.7 million-square-foot office tower was completed in 2020. The law firm moved from its previous offices at the MetLife Building at 200 Park Avenue, where its lease expired in 2021. The asking rent for the firm’s new expansion lease at One Vanderbilt was not disclosed, but Steven Durels, executive vice president and director of leasing and real property at SL Green, told Commercial Observer in February that rents in the building range from between $250 to “well over $300” per square foot. “Strong leasing momentum continues unabated with many tenants expanding and making significant capital investment to provide upscale work environments to better recruit and retain employee talent,” Durels said in a statement. CBRE’s Michael Monahan and Mark Ravesloot brokered the deal for Greenberg, while it’s unclear whether SL Green had any representation. Spokespeople for CBRE and Greenberg did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Greenberg’s expansion keeps One Vanderbilt at 100 percent leased. Other office tenants include TD Bank, investment management firm Carlyle Group, alternative investment firm Oak Hill Advisors and SL Green itself. News of the deal also comes during a recent wave of office leasing for SL Green, which said it has signed 129 office leases in Manhattan totaling 1.8 million square feet so far in 2026. bullets: Greenberg Traurig leases 33,477 SF additional space at One Vanderbilt, New York.
Expansion brings total law firm footprint to 133,365 SF; 10.5-year term secured.
Demonstrates trophy office tower strength despite broader Manhattan office sector headwinds.
stories.summary: Law firm Greenberg Traurig has signed a 10.5-year lease expansion for 33,477 additional square feet at SL Green's One Vanderbilt, bringing its total footprint in the 1.7 million-square-foot tower to 133,365 square feet. The firm originally signed a 15-year lease for four contiguous floors in January 2018 before the building opened in 2020, relocating from the MetLife Building when its lease expired in 2021. Terms were not disclosed, though SL Green previously indicated rents in the building range in the mid-$80s to low-$90s per square foot.
stories.impact: Trophy asset leasing strength in Midtown Manhattan signals tenant confidence in premium office space and SL Green's ability to retain and expand high-credit tenants despite the broader Manhattan office crisis. This does not reflect broad office demand; rather, it reinforces a bifurcated market where Class A trophy towers in central business districts command premium rents while secondary stock struggles. For multifamily: strong office tenant retention in CBD submarkets supports underlying neighborhood vitality and renter job stability, particularly in Midtown South.

stories.title: In Pro-Development South Florida, NIMBYism Rises
stories.excerpt: When Catherine Adler first moved to the West Palm Beach area in 1991, the South Florida city counted only a handful of high-rises, most of which were clustered around downtown. Today, though, she barely recognizes the regional city. Since 2019, at least nine towers have been completed. More than 10 are now under construction, some rising in residential neighborhoods packed with single-family homes. And more change is likely to come: Another nine developments have already been approved. “There’s cranes everywhere. You turn around and, all of a sudden, something’s going up,” Adler said. “The beautiful waterfront, the historic neighborhoods, and the charm — I don’t know if that’s going to be around.” South Florida has long been a bastion of new development. For decades, the region prospered thanks to pro-development policies that fueled a boom in condominium construction that attracted vacationers, retirees, foreign investors looking for a second home and wealthy newcomers. But, in recent years, South Florida has faced an all-too familiar obstacle: NIMBYism. The “Not In My Back Yard” phenomenon has long been common in places with starkly different politics, such as New York and California, but after years of developer free-for-all, NIMBYism has now finally descended onto South Florida. “We might be reaching a turning point,” said David Foster, an assistant professor at Florida State University who studies the politics of housing. “There’s nothing inherently partisan or conservative or liberal necessarily about homeowners’ opposition to development.” While South Florida, like most regions, has had its share of NIMBYism over the years, the movement is gaining significant steam since the COVID-19 pandemic, when millions of Northeasterners moved south to Florida. bullets: West Palm Beach, South Florida: 9 towers completed since 2019; 10+ under construction.
9 additional developments already approved; rising NIMBY opposition to high-rise residential.
Regional shift from decades of pro-development ethos due to growth concerns and historic preservation.
stories.summary: South Florida, long a bastion of pro-development policy fueling condo booms, faces mounting NIMBYism as neighborhood opposition intensifies. Since 2019, West Palm Beach has completed at least nine high-rises, with more than 10 currently under construction in predominantly single-family residential areas and another nine approved projects in the pipeline. Long-time residents cite loss of waterfront charm, historic character, and neighborhood density as catalysts for organized opposition to further vertical development.
stories.impact: South Florida's pivot toward NIMBY resistance creates regulatory risk and entitlement delays for multifamily developers, particularly in West Palm Beach and secondary residential corridors. Zoning and approval friction will likely extend development timelines and increase pre-development costs, reducing feasibility for mid-market projects. Developers should prioritize parcels with existing zoning or approved entitlements; expect policy tightening on height, setbacks, and affordable housing mandates in response to community pushback. Strong demand fundamentals remain, but cost to entitle will rise materially.

stories.title: Fed Raises Rates Quarter-Point, Signals Another Increase This Year
stories.excerpt: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point Wednesday, delivering its first increase since July 2023 as policymakers responded to renewed inflation pressures.  The unanimous decision by all 12 voting members of the Federal Open Market Committee lifted the federal funds rate’s target range to 3.75% to 4%.  Fed officials also signaled that additional tightening is likely. Eighteen of the 19 policymakers who submitted economic projections anticipated at least one more quarter-point increase by the end of the year. Four officials projected that rates would need to rise by another half percentage point in 2026, implying two additional quarter-point moves. The post Fed Raises Rates Quarter-Point, Signals Another Increase This Year appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Federal Open Market Committee votes unanimously to raise rates 25 bps to 3.75–4%.
18 of 19 officials project at least one more quarter-point hike by year-end 2026.
Four officials forecast additional 50 bps of tightening in 2026, implying two more 25 bp moves.
stories.summary: The Federal Reserve unanimously raised the federal funds rate target by 25 basis points to 3.75–4.0% on Wednesday, delivering its first increase since July 2023 in response to renewed inflation pressures. Economic projections submitted by policymakers show 18 of 19 officials expect at least one additional quarter-point increase by year-end, while four project a total of 50 basis points (two more quarter-point moves) in 2026. The move signals a shift from the prolonged hold period that preceded it.
stories.impact: Identical to Article 1; see impact statement above. Rate guidance directly affects SOFR-linked floating-rate financing and refinance demand for stabilized assets. Developers with bridge loans or ARMs should lock in fixed-rate term debt while spreads remain viable; those in early-stage projects should stress-test IRRs at 4.5–5.0% rates before committing capital.

stories.title: Cedar Park Offers Incentive Packages to Two Manufacturers
stories.excerpt: Cedar Park has agreed to economic incentives for two manufacturers who plan to spend over $40 million on their prospective businesses. Community Impact reports Machine Sciences Corporation is an Oregon-based company with existing operations in Florida that specializes in manufacturing complex, high-precision components for space, aerospace and defense industries. That includes parts for satellites, unmanned aerial vehicles and advanced defense systems. The city will pay the company $1 million if they spend $32 million at a Cedar Park facility by 2034 and hires 70 workers. Elite Metal Finishing provides services like chemical processing and plating, painting, non-destructive testing and parts marking for commercial, military and aerospace companies. Cedar Park will pay Elite Metal Finishing $750,000 if it spends $10 million and hires 170 employees. Both companies will lease space at the Cedar Tech I development near the northern border of Cedar Park. The post Cedar Park Offers Incentive Packages to Two Manufacturers appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Cedar Park, Texas offers $1.75M in incentives to two aerospace/defense manufacturers.
Machine Sciences Corp and Elite Metal Finishing plan $42M+ capex, 240+ job hires.
Both companies lease at Cedar Tech I development near Cedar Park's northern border.
stories.summary: Cedar Park, Texas has approved economic incentive packages totaling $1.75 million for two specialized manufacturers planning more than $42 million in capital investment. Machine Sciences Corporation, an Oregon-based aerospace and defense parts supplier with existing Florida operations, will receive $1 million if it invests $32 million and hires 70 workers by 2034. Elite Metal Finishing, providing aerospace and defense chemical processing services, will receive $750,000 for a $10 million investment and 170 hires. Both tenants will occupy space at the Cedar Tech I industrial development.
stories.impact: Cedar Park's recruitment of high-wage aerospace and defense manufacturing signals regional job diversification and attracts skilled worker in-migration to the Austin metro, bolstering underlying apartment demand across north Austin submarkets. Industrial tax incentives and public investment in Cedar Tech I create anchor tenants and workforce stability, supporting 10-year rent growth for Class A multifamily serving technical workers. Developers should focus on amenities and location near Cedar Park and the tech corridor; expect demographic skew toward mid-career professionals with higher rent-paying capacity.

stories.title: George Soros Puts Argonaut Building on the Market for Roughly $100M
stories.excerpt: Another Manhattan office building has hit the market. This time it’s the landmarked Argonaut Building, an approximately 140,000-square-foot office and retail building at 224 West 57th Street in Midtown. George Soros’s Soros Fund Management has put the property up for sale and is seeking a price of roughly $100 million, according to a source with knowledge of the deal. The 1909-built building between Broadway and Seventh Avenue seems to be fully occupied by Soros’s grant-making group the Open Society Foundations, which moved into the building in 2013 and has a lease running through 2042. TD Bank is a retail tenant on the ground floor. In April 2024, Soros, as a tenant, filed a foreclosure lawsuit against former landlord eretz group citing a default on a $145 million mortgage, The Real Deal reported at the time. Eretz had purchased the site for $213.8 million in 2015. It’s unclear why Soros is now looking to offload the property after winning it in a foreclosure auction, but the billionaire plans to move his grant-making group from the building once a deal is closed, according to TRD, which first reported the listing news. Newmark’s Adam Spies, Adam Doneger and Willis Robbins are marketing the building. An offering memo from the brokerage said the sale is a “rare opportunity” to reposition the historic building into “best-in-class residences,” TRD reported. The property has additional air rights that could give it a total buildable space of more than 200,000 square feet, according to the publication. If an office-to-residential conversion does proceed at the West 57th Street building, it would join another conversion project nearby at 135 East 57th Street, where TF Cornerstone is turning the former office building into 350 apartments. Newmark declined to comment, while a spokesperson for Open Society Foundations did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Isabelle Durso can be reached at idurso@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: George Soros lists Argonaut Building, Manhattan, for ~$100M; 140K SF office/retail.
Open Society Foundations lease runs through 2042; Soros plans tenant relocation post-sale.
Property acquired via foreclosure auction after Soros filed suit against previous landlord Eretz Group.
stories.summary: George Soros's Soros Fund Management has placed the landmarked Argonaut Building at 224 West 57th Street, Midtown, on the market at approximately $100 million. The 140,000-square-foot, 1909-built office and retail property is fully occupied by the Open Society Foundations (Soros's grant-making group) under a lease running through 2042, with TD Bank as a ground-floor retail tenant. Soros acquired the building through a foreclosure auction after filing suit against prior owner Eretz Group, which had purchased it for $213.8 million in 2015; Soros plans to relocate the Open Society Foundations once a buyer is found.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily relevance; this is an office asset sale signaling distress in Manhattan trophy office market. Indirect signal: Soros's willingness to liquidate a fully-leased office asset at 47% of Eretz Group's 2015 purchase price underscores the collapse in office valuations and refinance risk. For multifamily developers: confirms Manhattan office weakness creates supply risk (office-to-residential conversions), but also signals capital redeployment toward residential if conversion entitlements and economics improve.

stories.title: IMG Worldwide Renews 90K SF at SL Green’s 304 Park Avenue South
stories.excerpt: Global talent agency IMG Worldwide has renewed a 90,202-square-foot slice of its office lease at 304 Park Avenue South between East 22nd and East 23rd Streets in Midtown South. IMG arrived at SL Green Realty’s 12-story office building in 2008, according to CoStar Group. Its last reported expansion in 2016 saw the company occupy seven stories there, with its footprint growing to 130,655 square feet inside the 210,000-square-foot building. The company’s five-year renewal, announced by SL Green this week, may indicate a substantial downsizing in its offices at 304 Park Avenue South. It’s unclear whether IMG Worldwide will keep the rest of its footprint there. In early 2025, IMG Worldwide’s business lines shrunk dramatically after its parent company Endeavor sold off its sports media division and events portfolio. IMG Worldwide’s fashion and modeling businesses that are now held under WME Group, including IMG Models, continue to list offices at 304 Park Avenue South. A spokesperson for WME Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the deal. Terms of the 90,202-square-foot expansion were not disclosed, but Class B asking rents in Midtown South averaged $70.47 per square foot in August, according to Cushman & Wakefield data. Newmark’s Brian Goldman, Matthew Leon and Jason Perla represented IMG Worldwide in the renewal deal alongside Savills’ John Mambrino and David Providenti. It is unclear whether the landlord was represented in-house or by an outside brokerage. Other tenants at 304 Park Avenue South include retailers Bath & Body Works, restaurant chain Naya and Starbucks. Spokespeople for SL Green, Newmark and Savills did not respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: IMG Worldwide renews 90,202 SF at 304 Park Avenue South, Manhattan; five-year term.
Renewal indicates substantial downsizing from prior 130,655 SF footprint after Endeavor divestiture.
Company's media division sold; fashion/modeling operations continue under WME Group umbrella.
stories.summary: Global talent agency IMG Worldwide has renewed a five-year lease for 90,202 square feet at SL Green's 304 Park Avenue South in Midtown South, a significant reduction from its prior 130,655-square-foot occupancy across seven stories. The renewal follows major restructuring of IMG's parent company Endeavor, which divested its sports media division and events portfolio in early 2025. IMG's remaining fashion and modeling businesses now operate under WME Group and continue to maintain office space at 304 Park Avenue South, though terms were not disclosed.
stories.impact: IMG's downsizing reflects corporate contraction and portfolio streamlining post-divestiture, signaling broader talent agency consolidation in Midtown South. While this is office-sector news, it highlights corporate restructuring risk and tenant flight risk in media/entertainment-dependent office markets. For multifamily developers in Manhattan and LA (media hubs): watch for downstream job losses and downstream demand softening if agency consolidation accelerates; corporate vacating typically precedes renter out-migration in 12–18 months.

stories.title: San Antonio Investor Scores Financing for 312-Unit Rental Asset
stories.excerpt: Strategic Property Investment has secured a $40.3 million loan for Birwood Heights, a 312-unit community in San Antonio. Multihousing News reports the non-recourse bridge loan features a three-year initial term with a stabilized 6.45 percent debt yield and 80 percent LTV, which would value the property at $50.4 million. Birwood Heights was delivered in 2019. It features one- to three-bedroom floor plans that average 975 square feet. The community’s amenities include a swimming pool, gym, outdoor grilling areas and resident lounges. Located at 4003 N. Loop 1604 W. on more than 27 acres, the property is less than 5 miles from Interstate 10, within San Antonio’s north submarket. USAA’s headquarters, the South Texas Medical Center and The University of Texas at San Antonio. are all nearby. IPA Capital Markets’ Brandon Roth, Adam Mengacci and Travis Headapohl arranged the debt placement. The post San Antonio Investor Scores Financing for 312-Unit Rental Asset appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Strategic Property Investment secures $40.3M bridge loan for Birwood Heights, San Antonio.
312-unit stabilized community (2019 delivery) financed at 6.45% yield, 80% LTV.
Property located in north San Antonio submarket near USAA HQ, UT-San Antonio, medical center.
stories.summary: Strategic Property Investment has obtained a $40.3 million non-recourse bridge loan for Birwood Heights, a stabilized 312-unit apartment community in San Antonio's north submarket. The three-year bridge features a 6.45% debt yield and 80% LTV, implying an asset value of approximately $50.4 million. Delivered in 2019 and located on 27+ acres at 4003 N. Loop 1604 W., the community is proximate to USAA headquarters, UT-San Antonio, and the South Texas Medical Center. Units average 975 square feet across one- to three-bedroom plans.
stories.impact: Bridge financing at 6.45% yield for stabilized assets signals refinance headwinds and limited agency financing appetite; 80% LTV is conservative, reflecting lender caution on debt recovery. San Antonio's strong anchors (USAA, healthcare, university) support stable occupancy, but the bridge structure suggests owner equity constraints or rate-lock concerns ahead of anticipated refinance. For developers: San Antonio remains a strong multifamily market due to employment diversity, but expect reduced leverage and higher cost of capital; focus on stabilized assets with strong underlying demand to justify refinance risk.

stories.title: Proligis Offloads Fully-Leased 604K-SF Denver Airport Industrial Property
stories.excerpt: Prologis has sold The Collection at Airport Central, a fully-leased, five-building industrial portfolio totaling 604,429 square feet in Denver’s Airport Central micro-market to Berkeley Partners. The portfolio was 100% leased at the time of sale and includes a diversified roster of 12 tenants across five strategically located industrial assets. Jeremy Ballenger, Tyler Carner and Keiffer Garton of CBRE represented Prologis in the transaction. The assets feature a mix of multi-tenant and single-tenant configurations designed to accommodate a broad range of industrial users. The portfolio is leased to tenants across industries, including logistics, distribution, building products, manufacturing, business services, trade show logistics, records management and e-commerce fulfillment. Through the first quarter of 2026, Denver’s industrial market recorded 64 consecutive quarters of positive net absorption, while Airport Central maintained some of the lowest vacancy levels and strongest rent growth among Denver industrial submarkets. The post Proligis Offloads Fully-Leased 604K-SF Denver Airport Industrial Property appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Prologis sells Collection at Airport Central, Denver (604K SF, 5 buildings) to Berkeley Partners.
Portfolio 100% leased at sale; 12 tenants across logistics, distribution, manufacturing, e-commerce.
Denver Airport Central submarket: 64 consecutive quarters positive absorption, lowest vacancy, strong rent growth.
stories.summary: Prologis has divested The Collection at Airport Central, a fully-leased, five-building industrial portfolio totaling 604,429 square feet in Denver's Airport Central micro-market, to Berkeley Partners. The portfolio was 100% leased at close and includes 12 tenants across a diversified roster spanning logistics, distribution, building products, manufacturing, records management, and e-commerce fulfillment. Denver's Airport Central submarket has recorded 64 consecutive quarters of positive net absorption through Q1 2026 and maintains some of the lowest vacancy and strongest rent growth among Denver industrial submarkets.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact; this is industrial asset sale. Indirect signal: Prologis's willingness to exit a 100%-leased, strong-performing asset in a supply-constrained submarket suggests capital redeployment toward higher-return opportunities or balance sheet optimization. For multifamily: Denver Airport Central strength reflects underlying job and logistics growth; nearby residential markets (particularly north metro) should benefit from tenant workforce demand and in-migration. Watch for Denver North submarket (residential) to absorb displaced logistics workers and see sustained rent growth.

stories.title: 29th Street Trades Aurora Apartment Community for $72.5M
stories.excerpt: 29th Street Capital sold the Peakline at Copperleaf apartments for $72.5 million, a significant dip from the price the company paid for the property four years ago. The company paid $104 million from the development iin 2022. Multifamily News reports that the Michelson Organization acquired the property with the help of a $30.6 million five-year Fannie Mae loan. Located at 4343 S. Picadilly St., it sits just off Picadilly Street and East Quincy Avenue. Peakline at Copperleaf comprises one-, two- and three-bedroom units, with floorplans ranging from 732 to 1,232 square feet. All units feature private balconies or patios, with direct access garages available in select units. Common-area amenities at the pet-friendly community include a fitness center, bocce ball court, clubhouse, outdoor kitchen with grilling stations, swimming pool, spa, pet wash and dog park. The property also has some 550 parking spaces at ground level. The post 29th Street Trades Aurora Apartment Community for $72.5M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: 29th Street Capital sells Peakline at Copperleaf, Aurora, Colorado for $72.5M (down from $104M 2022).
312-unit asset purchased with $30.6M five-year Fannie Mae loan by Michelson Organization.
30% price decline in four years reflects cap rate compression, financing stress, or demand softness.
stories.summary: 29th Street Capital has sold Peakline at Copperleaf, a 312-unit apartment community in Aurora, Colorado, to the Michelson Organization for $72.5 million—a 30% discount from the $104 million 29th Street paid for the development in 2022. Michelson acquired the property with $30.6 million in Fannie Mae financing on a five-year term. The property, located at 4343 S. Picadilly St., features one- to three-bedroom units (732–1,232 SF), amenities including fitness center, bocce ball court, pool, spa, and 550 ground-level parking spaces.
stories.impact: Sharp price decline signals value destruction from rate environment and financing repricing since 2022; 29th Street's forced sale at 30% markdown reflects bridge or mezzanine debt maturity stress and refinance risk on fixed-rate debt issued in a lower-rate environment. For developers: Aurora market remains challenging post-pandemic overbuilding; Fannie Mae's willingness to lend at $30.6M (~42% LTV) signals stabilized fundamentals but constrained valuation. This transaction underscores refinance risk for 2022–2023 acquisitions; lock in fixed-rate term debt immediately if bridge exposure exists. Monitor Aurora's supply/demand balance closely—continued developer distress may suppress new starts.
